nameStory: This delicate gull is named after Napoleon's nephew, Charles Lucien Bonaparte, a 19th-century ornithologist who studied North American birds. Unlike his famous uncle who conquered Europe, Charles Bonaparte conquered the world of bird science, describing many new species including this graceful little gull.
description: Bonaparte's Gull is one of New England's smallest and most elegant gulls, measuring just 11-15 inches from beak to tail. In summer, adults sport a striking jet-black hood that makes them look like they're wearing a dark cap, while their bodies remain crisp white with soft gray wings. During fall and winter, the black hood disappears, leaving just a dark spot behind the eye. These petite gulls have a buoyant, almost tern-like flight that sets them apart from their bulkier gull cousins.

idTips.label: Black hood in breeding season
idTips.description: Adults develop a complete slate-black hood from May through August that covers the entire head and upper neck, creating a dramatic contrast with their white body

idTips.label: Small, delicate size
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller and more petite than other common gulls, with a thin, needle-like black bill that looks almost too delicate for a gull

idTips.label: Light, buoyant flight
idTips.description: Flies with quick, almost butterfly-like wingbeats that are much more rapid and graceful than the heavy flapping of larger gulls

idTips.label: Winter dark ear spot
idTips.description: When not in breeding plumage, shows a distinctive dark smudge behind the eye like someone dabbed them with a gray marker

idTips.label: Gray wing pattern
idTips.description: Wings appear pale gray above with clean white trailing edges that flash prominently in flight, lacking the heavy black wingtips of many larger gulls

habitat: Bonaparte's Gulls favor open coastal waters, large bays, and harbors throughout New England's coastline. You'll often spot them feeding over deeper waters offshore, though they also visit large inland lakes and reservoirs during migration. They prefer areas with good fish populations and frequently associate with mixed flocks of other gulls and terns.

seasonality.spring: Migrants arrive in April and May, with birds transitioning into their dramatic black breeding hoods. Peak numbers occur during migration as birds head to northern breeding grounds.
seasonality.summer: Some non-breeding individuals may linger along the coast in full black-hooded breeding plumage, though most have moved north to nest in Canada and Alaska.
seasonality.fall: September through November brings the largest numbers as migrants return south, now mostly in winter plumage with just the telltale dark ear spots.
seasonality.winter: Smaller numbers overwinter along the coast, particularly in harbors and bays, showing clean white heads with dark ear patches and maintaining their delicate appearance.

funFact: Unlike most gulls that nest on the ground, Bonaparte's Gulls are the only North American gull species that regularly builds stick nests high up in conifer trees, sometimes 20 feet off the ground - making them the 'tree gulls' of the bird world!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with the much rarer Black-headed Gull, but Bonaparte's Gull has a completely black hood in breeding plumage while Black-headed Gull's hood is actually chocolate brown. In winter, Bonaparte's shows a cleaner, smaller dark ear spot compared to Black-headed Gull's more extensive dark markings.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called Bonaparte's Gull, this species was actually first described by George Ord in 1815, but he named it in honor of Charles Lucien Bonaparte's contributions to ornithology. The scientific name 'philadelphia' refers to where the first specimen was collected, not where the species commonly occurs.
compareHints: Bonaparte's Gull is much smaller and more delicate than its closest New England relative, the Black-headed Gull. Bonaparte's has a thinner bill, more buoyant flight, and in breeding plumage shows a solid black hood versus the Black-headed Gull's chocolate-brown hood. Bonaparte's also lacks the prominent white wing flashes that Black-headed Gulls display in flight.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative Bonaparte's Gull, the Black-headed Gull is slightly larger and stockier with a more robust build.
